Explain why the tritone earned the nickname 'diabolus in musica', what makes this interval sound so restless and unresolved, and how it later became essential to blues, jazz and heavy metal.
Explain why flashbulb memories of shocking public events feel vividly certain yet drift dramatically over the years, as studies of people's recollections of the Challenger disaster revealed.

Explain differential privacy for a reader who has never written a line of code, showing how adding carefully calibrated random noise to statistics lets a census learn about a population without revealing anything about any single person in it.

topic: a crow that remembers a face
prompt: Write a brief story about a crow who remembers the face of a person who once trapped it and, years later, leads its whole family to scold that person in the street.

topic: a seed from the Svalbard vault
prompt: Write a brief story set centuries in the future, in which a child plants a seed retrieved from the Svalbard Global Seed Vault and grows a crop that no one alive has ever tasted.
Explain al-Ghazali's example of cotton brought into contact with fire, and his argument that we never actually observe the fire causing the burning, only one event regularly accompanying another.
Explain how bee orchids deceive male bees by mimicking the look, feel and scent of a female, tricking them into carrying pollen without offering any reward.

topic: diffusion models denoising static into images
prompt: Write a lyrical description of how an AI diffusion model creates a picture, starting from pure television static and removing noise step by step until a recognizable scene emerges, like a photograph slowly developing in a darkroom tray.

Argue whether a person who was as morally good as possible in every action would be someone to admire, or whether, as Susan Wolf suggested, such a moral saint would lack something essential to a good life.

topic: Harvard Mark II moth, first bug
prompt: Write a vivid scene describing the day in 1947 when operators of the Harvard Mark II computer found a moth trapped in one of its relays and taped it into the logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found.'

Explain how thousands of starlings in a murmuration move as a single rippling shape without any leader, each bird responding only to its nearest handful of neighbours, in prose that captures the wonder of watching it over a marsh at dusk.

topic: cosmic ray bit flips in memory
prompt: Explain how high-energy particles from space can flip a single bit inside a computer's memory, referencing the 2003 Belgian election in which one candidate inexplicably gained exactly 4,096 extra votes, and how engineers guard against such invisible strikes.

topic: axial tilt as cause of seasons
prompt: Explain why Earth has seasons, gently correcting the widespread belief that summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.
Describe how, in 1932, Bell Labs engineer Karl Jansky, hunting for sources of static that troubled transatlantic telephone calls, found a faint hiss coming from the center of the Milky Way.

topic: Buridan's ass and perfectly balanced choice
prompt: Explain the puzzle of Buridan's ass, the perfectly rational donkey that starves between two identical bales of hay, and what it reveals about choosing when reasons are perfectly balanced.

topic: Pando, the aspen that is one organism
prompt: Write a lyrical description of walking through Pando in Utah, a grove of tens of thousands of quaking aspens that are all one organism sharing a single ancient root system, while its leaves tremble gold in the autumn wind.

Explain digital steganography, the art of hiding a secret message inside an ordinary-looking photograph by subtly altering the least significant bits of its pixels, and how its goal differs from that of encryption.
Write a reflective passage about Pando, the grove of quaking aspen in Utah that is actually a single organism with tens of thousands of trunks sharing one root system.

Explain the 'Great Dimming' of Betelgeuse in 2019–2020, when the red supergiant faded noticeably and fuelled speculation that it was about to explode, and what astronomers concluded had actually happened.

Explain how Henrietta Swan Leavitt, working as a poorly paid human 'computer' at Harvard Observatory, discovered that the pulsing rhythm of certain stars reveals their true brightness, giving astronomers their first yardstick for measuring the universe.

Explain the geological theory that the trances of the Pythia, the priestess of the Oracle at Delphi, were induced by sweet-smelling gases rising from fault lines beneath Apollo's temple, and why the idea is still debated.

topic: starlight as a message from the past
prompt: Explain why looking up at the night sky is really looking into the past, since the light reaching your eyes from some stars set out before your great-grandparents were born, in a tone of quiet astonishment.
Describe what happens inside a chrysalis as a caterpillar dissolves much of its body into a soup of cells and rebuilds itself as a butterfly.

Write an explanatory passage about hemispatial neglect, the condition in which a stroke patient may eat only the right half of their plate and draw clocks with all twelve numbers crowded onto one side.

topic: Inge Lehmann and Earth's inner core
prompt: Explain how the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann, studying faint seismic waves from a 1929 earthquake, deduced in 1936 that Earth has a solid inner core hidden within its liquid outer core.

Explain how the first message sent over ARPANET in October 1969 was supposed to read 'LOGIN' but crashed the system after two letters, and how the idea of packet switching made the network that grew into the internet possible.

Explain how group theory describes the Rubik's Cube and how mathematicians proved that every one of its 43 quintillion scrambled positions can be solved in twenty moves or fewer, a figure nicknamed 'God's number.'

Explain the Gale–Shapley stable matching algorithm, why it always produces pairings in which no two people would both rather abandon their partners for each other, and how a version of it now matches new doctors to hospitals.
Explain the incongruity theory of humor, associated with thinkers like Kant and Schopenhauer, showing how laughter springs from the sudden collapse of an expectation into something absurd.
Explain the phenomenon of ant mills, in which army ants blindly following pheromone trails can become trapped in a circling death spiral, and what it reveals about the limits of simple rules.

topic: Epictetus and the Stoic dichotomy of control
prompt: Explain the Stoic dichotomy of control as taught by Epictetus, a philosopher who had once been enslaved, and how separating what is up to us from what is not was meant to make a person unshakable.
Write a short reflective passage about kintsugi, the Japanese art of mending broken pottery with gold-dusted lacquer, using it as a metaphor for how people carry their own repaired fractures.
Describe, in the second person, standing on a misty mountain ridge with the Sun at your back and seeing your own giant shadow cast on the clouds, ringed by a rainbow halo called a glory.
Describe what it would be like to climb Olympus Mons on Mars, a volcano so vast and gently sloped that its summit would lie beyond the horizon for someone standing at its base.
Explain who 'Mitochondrial Eve' was and why she was neither the first woman nor the only woman alive in her time.

topic: perceiving the world by bat echolocation
prompt: Describe what it would be like to perceive the world through echolocation as a bat, hunting moths in the dark by listening to the shapes of returning echoes.

Explain Hannah Arendt's phrase 'the banality of evil,' coined while she observed the trial of Adolf Eichmann, and why her suggestion that great harm can flow from thoughtless obedience unsettled so many readers.
Write a lyrical monologue in the voice of an old manual typewriter gathering dust in an attic, which remembers every love letter, unfinished novel and rejection notice it ever struck onto paper.
Explain why comets often show two distinct tails, one of dust and one of ions, and why both point away from the Sun even when the comet is heading outward.
Explain to a curious ten-year-old why you get a little electric shock when you touch a doorknob after shuffling across a carpet, especially on dry winter days.

topic: Galois's final night before the duel
prompt: Write an evocative passage imagining the night before twenty-year-old Évariste Galois's fatal duel in 1832, as he hurriedly scrawled his mathematical ideas into a final letter to a friend.
Describe the moment in 1923 when Edwin Hubble, studying a photographic plate of the Andromeda 'nebula,' crossed out an 'N' and scrawled 'VAR!', realizing it was a whole galaxy far beyond our own.
Describe what Earth might have looked like during a Snowball Earth episode, when ice may have reached nearly to the equator and life clung on in hidden refuges.
Describe Welwitschia mirabilis in the Namib Desert, a plant that grows only two leaves in its entire life of a thousand years or more, letting them fray into ribbons across the sand.

Explain why Jeremy Bentham insisted that the question about animals is not whether they can reason or talk but whether they can suffer, and how this reframing reshaped moral thinking about other species.

topic: how general anesthesia switches off consciousness
prompt: Explain what scientists currently understand about how general anesthesia switches off consciousness, and why it remains remarkable that doctors can reliably make a mind vanish and return without fully knowing how.

topic: St. Elmo's fire on ship masts
prompt: Describe the eerie blue-violet glow of St. Elmo's fire crackling on the masts of a sailing ship during a storm, and the physics of electrical discharge behind it.
Write a short story about Johannes Kepler's years-long 'war with Mars,' ending at the moment he realizes the planet's orbit is not a circle but an ellipse.
